# Lawmakers pass dozens of bills as 2026 session wraps up
![](https://www.cpr.org/cdn-cgi/image/width=3840,quality=75,format=auto/https://wp-cpr.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2026/05/260513-COLORADO-STATE-LEGISLATURE-LAST-DAY-OF-SESSION-SINE-DIE-COPOLITICS-KEVINJBEATY-61.jpg)
Kevin J. Beaty/Denverite
In the waning hours of the 2026 Colorado legislative session Wednesday, state lawmakers pushed dozens of bills over the finish line bringing the total number of bills sent to the governor up to nearly 450, according to nonpartisan legislative staff. But, more than 100 bills either failed on the chamber floors or withered on the branch as the clock ran out.

With lawmakers limited by an exceptionally [tight budget](https://www.cpr.org/2026/04/01/colorado-budget-draft-billion-shortfall-2026/) and a [lame duck governor](https://www.cpr.org/podcast-episode/colorado-governor-jared-polis-final-year-purplish/), any high-stakes political battles were resolved weeks ago. But lawmakers still made a few big moves on the final day of session, known as sine die.
Moderate Democrats joined Republicans to kill a progressive proposal to establish state-level worker safety protections meant to fill a gap left by a weakened federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) under President Trump.

Progressive Democratic Senator Katie Wallace of Longmont, who sponsored that bill, said she was disappointed it failed, but that it’s part of serving in a legislature with such a large number of Democrats.

Republicans on Capitol Hill are poised to clash in the lame duck over how far to push President Trump’s agenda.

Midterm voters are widely expected to give Democrats control of the House, and maybe the Senate, in the next Congress, which would bring Trump’s legislative agenda to a screeching halt beginning next year.
